transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Windsor Johnston.
President Trump's agreement to import millions of tons of Russian diesel
is drawing criticism from members of Congress and U.S. allies.
The deal follows his administration's decision to lift sanctions
imposed in response to Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
NPR's Mara Laison reports the imports are unlikely
to lower diesel prices right away.
He is trying, without much success yet,
to bring down oil prices before election day.
He blames Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries
for higher gas prices in the U.S.,
even though it's the Iran war that is causing higher prices in the U.S.
And he has demanded that Ukraine stop bombing Russian oil refineries.
He hasn't demanded that Russia stop bombing Ukrainian energy infrastructure,
its electrical grid, or civilian targets.
That's NPR's Mara Laison reporting.
A federal judge is ordering the Trump administration
to temporarily stop airing its taxpayer-funded ads that promote the president.
They've been airing in recent weeks ahead of the November midterms.
NPR's Luke Garrett reports a U.S. District Court judge
is banning the ads for two weeks while a court case continues.
Judge Roshan ordered the Trump administration to pull its multimillion-dollar ad buy,
no later than Sunday night.
The ruling came after a coalition, including the nonprofit Common Cause,
challenged the taxpayer-funded Trump ads in New York federal court,
arguing it violated congressional appropriation and government propaganda rules.
The White House had set aside $20 million for the taxpayer-funded Trump ads' court record show.
The campaign-styled ads began airing in September,
sparking bipartisan concern.
Trump himself acknowledged the backlash in early October,
saying he'd pay for the ads himself.
Despite this, the commercials, which feature Trump and his political agenda,
continued to air nationwide.
The White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the judge's order.
Luke Garrett, NPR News, Washington.
Pope Leo is set to have surgery this week to remove a growth on his lung.
NPR's Ava Pukach reports lung nodules are common in older adults.
Dr. Panikis Goliassatus, a pulmonary physician at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine,
says the majority of lung nodules are benign, calling them the lung's wrinkles.
He says once a nodule is discovered, doctors then test it to see if there is cause for concern.
For the Pope to have had some imaging done that found him to have a lung nodule,
where they're now discussing removing it, means he likely had some findings
that resulted in some level of concern outside of the size.
The Vatican says the surgery will occur at Rome's Jamely Hospital,
and the Pope will have a week of recovery.
Ava Pukach, NPR News.
This is NPR News in Washington.
Hurricane Simon is bringing heavy rain and dangerous winds to Mexico's Pacific Coast.
It weakened to a Category 3 overnight with wind speeds of about 115 miles per hour,
but remains a dangerous storm.
Floodwaters have entered homes along the coast.
Authorities have evacuated vulnerable communities and opened emergency shelters.
Forecasters are warning of life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in mountainous areas.
The U.S. is in the midst of the biggest and deadliest measles epidemic in decades.
With cases reported across the country, infectious disease experts say
some vaccinated adults should consider another measles shot.
NPR's Maria Godoy has more.
Before vaccines, measles used to kill four to five hundred people in the U.S. each year.
Two doses of the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine is 97 percent effective.
Most people vaccinated before 1989 probably received just one dose
instead of the two doses recommended for children today.
Dr. Larry Kociolek of Northwestern University says traditionally
one dose has been considered sufficient protection for adults not at high risk.
But he says these days...
If you are living in areas with high measles activity,
it does make a whole lot of sense for adults to go ahead and get that second dose.
If you're not sure of your vaccination history, he says there's no harm
in getting an extra dose of the MMR vaccine.
Maria Godoy, NPR News.
This is NPR News in Washington.

topics.text: President Trump agrees to import millions of tons of Russian diesel, drawing congressional and ally criticism
Federal judge temporarily bans Trump administration's taxpayer-funded ads promoting the president ahead of midterms
Pope Leo to undergo surgery in Rome to remove a lung growth; benign nodules common in older adults
Hurricane Simon weakens to Category 3, bringing flooding and dangerous winds to Mexico's Pacific Coast
U.S. in biggest, deadliest measles epidemic in decades; experts urge some vaccinated adults get second dose
